newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu names arch-rival to head Zaire government.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu names arch-rival to head Zaire government.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko on Wednesday formally approved the appointment of his arch-rival Etienne Tshisekedi as prime minister to steer Zaire through civil war.

State radio announced the appointment as the U.N. refugee agency started repatriating 3,000 Rwandan Hutu war refugees from Zaire and a U.N. investigator accused rebels of massacring the Hutus last year.
"The president of the republic ratifies and names Tshisekedi wa Mulumba as Prime Minister and head of the transitional government," the radio said.
Mobutu's spokesman Kabuya Lumuna confirmed the radio report. "The decree has been signed," Kabuya told Reuters.
He said a meeting between the two men was arranged earlier on Wednesday evening, but he could not confirm whether it had taken place.
Constitutionally Mobutu was simply charged with signing an endorsement of a candidate chosen by parliament.

Lawmakers on Tuesday nominated Tshisekedi, a former prime minister sacked by Mobutu in 1993, to head the government and steer Zaire through negotiations with rebels who hold a quarter of the vast Central African country.
Tshisekedi has long favoured talks with rebel chief Laurent Kabila to end the war launched from eastern Zaire in October.
But the rebels are pressing on with their military campaign in which they have put the demoralised Zaire army on the run, and many Zaireans believe Tshisekedi will be Mobutu's last prime minister.

Peter Kessler, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Goma city, said the agency expected to have repatriated 3,000 Hutu refugees by truck to Rwanda from Karuba by the end of Wednesday.
Aid officials said 20,000 refugees remained at Karuba west of Goma and they expected sites at Tingi Tingi and Amisi were emptied of refugees by two flights on Wednesday to Goma .

Kessler said the highest death rate appeared to be at km 82 (mile 50) south of the rebel-held northeastern capital of Kisangani where about half the 800 refugees there in mid-March had died of malnutrition, malaria, sickness and their wounds.
He said aid agency staff clearing shelters at Lula, seven km (four miles) south of Kisangani, found 50 bodies on Monday of refugees who had died from exhaustion, sickness or malnutrition.

The rebels ordered 20,000 refugees to leave Lula on Monday and join another 60,000 farther south of Kisangani for security reasons. The rebels fear they include former Rwandan Hutu troops and militiamen who fought alongside Zairean government troops.
In Geneva, a U.N. human rights investigator accused the rebels of massacring Rwandan refugees during their push across the region late last year and urged a speedy investigation.
Roberto Garreton said on his return from a three-day visit to Goma that the rebels had failed to come up with satisfactory answers to allegations of killings, torture and disappearances.

At a news conference, Garreton said eyewitness accounts of the number of people killed by the rebels ranged from hundreds to 50,000 and demanded a detailed probe by independent experts to be appointed by the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.
"There were massacres by the rebels. That's for sure. There's an enormous list of allegations of massacres but it is impossible to give numbers," the Chilean investigator said.
Zaire accuses Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army and Ugandan troops of supporting the rebels, but they deny these charges.

"I can't say that the Rwandan and Ugandan armies are there with their generals and colonels. But the local people view the rebel forces as an occupation army. It is clear that these rebels are not Zaireans," Garreton said.
